Progress note:
I built the app as a standalone page: [circuit-diagram.html](circuit-diagram.html). It's open in the Preview tab now, starting with a sample series circuit.

**What it does**
- **Parts palette:** wire, battery, resistor, capacitor, inductor, switch, voltmeter, ammeter, and a rotatable current arrow. Tap a part, then tap the dot grid to place it; drag parts to move; rotate with the toolbar or <kbd>R</kbd>.
- **Drawing wires:** drag between two dots, or tap one dot then a second one. Wires connect anything they touch, including crossed wires and part terminals.
- **Editable values:** battery voltage (or a **Current** source mode where you enter amps), resistor resistance, and switch open/closed. Changes update the drawing and readings immediately.
- **Live meters:** a real modified-nodal-analysis solver computes the circuit from the drawn topology. The voltmeter shows potential difference, the ammeter shows branch current, and readings appear both on the symbol and in the inspector. Capacitors are open and inductors are shorts for steady DC; batteries include a negligible 0.05 Ω internal resistance so odd source arrangements stay well-behaved.
- **Mobile-first layout:** dot-snapped touch drawing, large palette buttons, a palette pinned to the bottom of the screen, a sticky header, safe-area insets, and the inspector scrolls itself above the palette. The page fits a 390×844 viewport without horizontal scrolling.
- **Theme:** follows the system on first visit, toggles from the header, remembers the choice, and uses the MU green/gold palette. The board autosaves to localStorage, and there's undo, delete, clear, and a load-example action.

**Verified in the browser**
- Sample 9 V / 100 Ω → **90.0 mA** on the ammeter and **9.00 V** on the voltmeter.
- Changing the battery to 12 V → 120 mA and 12.0 V immediately (fixed a stale-reading bug found during testing).
- Switch open → 0 A / 0 V; closed → readings return.
- Current-source mode set to 0.5 A → 500 mA and 50.0 V.
- Capacitor in series → 0 A with full voltage across it; inductor in series → normal current, 0 V across it.
- Wire drawing by drag and by two taps, rotate/delete/undo, clear/undo, theme persistence, board reload persistence, and 360×640, 390×844, and 1280×900 layouts. No console errors.

I left [index.html](index.html) untouched, so the chemistry hub still works as before; the new tool is just an additional page you can link from the Physics menu. Nothing was committed.

One thing to flag first: your message says "the torque experiment", but the attached file is **Exp 06a – Work and Power**, so I built that experiment — the torque one you attached last time already exists as `physics/torque-balance.html`. **The app** — [physics/work-power-lab.html](physics/work-power-lab.html), one self-contained page, no dependencies, reachable from the hub's Physics menu as **Work & Power Lab (incline)**.

- **The rig:** a wooden board on a stand with a pulley at the raised end, a cart on the board, and a string over the pulley to a hanging weight. Set the board length and raised-end height (which fixes sinθ), the distance the cart travels, the cart mass, the hanger mass and the weight added. The stop mark is draggable along the board, and everything recomputes live.
- **The run:** press **Release the cart**. The cart accelerates, the hanger drops, and the clock stops at the mark. Nine trials in all — three mass groups × three trials, exactly as the file asks, with the trials auto-advancing to the next mass as each fills up.
- **Timing:** **Photo-gate** (exact crossing time) or **Stopwatch**, where you tap Stop yourself and your reaction is part of the reading. In stopwatch mode, letting the cart reach the end of the board without pressing voids the trial, just as "be sure to stop the cart so it will not fly off the incline" implies.
- **The forces are shown on the cart:** the pull from the hanging weight, the cart's weight along the slope, and (in Realistic) rolling resistance — so the reason you must "add weights until the cart starts moving" is visible. The app names the threshold: with the default rig it needs ≥ 125 g in the Idal model, ≥ 134.7 g with rolling resistance.
- **Record sheet** reproduces the file's Data table (Mass added, Total mass, Trial 1–3, Average) plus the recorded hanger mass, distance traveled, height the cart rises and cart mass, each in g/kg and cm/m as the sheet wants.
- **Post-lab analysis** answers Q1–Q9 per mass with the arithmetic shown: v<sub>avg</sub> = d/t̄, a = 2d/t̄², v<sub>f</sub> = 2d/t̄, F = m<sub>total</sub> g, W = F d, P = W/t̄, W<sub>cons</sub> = ΔPE = m<sub>cart</sub> g h, ΔKE = ½m<sub>cart</sub>v<sub>f</sub>², and then whether the system is conservative or not, with the non-conservative work called out.
- **Dark/light toggle** in the header, remembered, following the system on a first visit; the drawing has its own dark palette. Board labels scale up on phones (11.8–12.5 px at 390 px wide), the run button stays pinned in the sticky instrument panel, and the page never scrolls sideways from 320 px to desktop.

**Measured in the browser** (defaults: cart 500 g, hanger 50 g, 120 cm board raised 30 cm, d = 50 cm)

- Ideal, photo-gate — Mass 1 (200 g added, 250 g total): a = **1.633 m/s²**, crossing at **0.782 s**, v<sub>avg</sub> **0.639**, v<sub>f</sub> **1.279 m/s**, F **2.450 N**, W **1.225 J**, P **1.566 W**, ΔPE **0.613 J**, ΔKE **0.409 J**; W − (ΔKE + ΔPE) = 0.204 J, exactly the hanger's own kinetic energy, and the balance closes to 0.000 J once the hanger is included → "the system is conservative".
- Mass 2 (350 g): **0.621 s**, W **1.715 J**, P **2.762 W**, ΔKE **0.648 J**. Mass 3 (450 g): **0.546 s**, W **2.205 J**, P **4.038 W**, ΔKE **0.839 J**.
- Realistic, μ = 0.02 — Mass 1: **0.815 s**, a **1.506 m/s²**; the leftover energy is **0.0479 J** against a predicted f d = **0.0474 J** → "non-conservative, that is the work done against rolling resistance".
- Stopwatch, pressing about 0.2 s late: recorded **1.008 s** where the true crossing was **0.815 s**, and the verdict correctly splits the leftover 0.243 J into 0.047 J of friction plus ≈0.196 J of timing effect rather than blaming friction for all of it — the one conclusion a real stopwatch run can't reach by hand.
- Too little weight (100 g total): the cart refuses to start, the app reports pull 0.98 N against slope pull 1.23 N and says to add ≥ 25 g more, and no trial is recorded.
- Also checked: a 30° board with the cart travelling the full 120 cm (nothing leaves the canvas), the 9-trial flow and auto-advance, per-row and global clearing, the model/timing toggles mirroring between the run bar and the model card, theme in both directions, persistence of trials, settings and theme across a reload, and no console errors.

Bugs I found and fixed while testing: the cart group was parented to the SVG root instead of the rotated board group, so the cart was being drawn off-canvas; the status chips didn't refresh when a run started; the stopwatch path passed centimetres into a recorder expecting metres; the force labels and angle label collided and overflowed the canvas edge; the "start" label was hidden behind the cart.

Limitations worth knowing: the hanger's descent in the drawing is schematic (compressed 1.5 px/cm against the board's 6.33), so the visual drop isn't to scale even though the distance is. The sheet's two simplifications are stated in the footer and in the analysis — the pull is taken as the hanging weight, whereas a real string pulls with T = m<sub>hanger</sub>(g − a), and Q8's kinetic energy is the cart's alone, which is why that row's leftover is exactly the hanger's KE. {"kind":"tool","id":"fnBfvv3t9vs","toolName":"write_file","input":{"path":"atwood-machine/README.md","instructions":"Project README for the Atwood's machine app.","content":"# Atwood's Machine Lab · Photogate

Two masses on either side of a pulley, connected by a light string, timed with a photogate. Fit
velocity against time to get the acceleration, then relate that acceleration to the mass difference
and to the total mass.

**Run it:** open [index.html](index.html) in any browser. It is one self-contained file — no build
step, no dependencies, works offline and on a phone. Dark/light is the button in the header and is
remembered.

## What it does

- **The apparatus:** a ring stand and clamp holding a pulley with a photogate straddling its rim,
  two masses hanging from the string and a cm ruler showing the descent. Release the masses and the
  heavier side falls while the pulley spins and the gate pulses once per spoke.
- **The photogate is the measurement.** Velocity is sampled once every tenth of a turn of the pulley
  — one sample per 1.60 cm of string, what the Ultra Pulley's 10-spoke groove gives — and a
  least-squares line is fitted to those points, as the *Curve Fit → Linear* step does. The slope is
  the acceleration; the fit's intercept, r² and sample count (about 28 per run) are reported.
- **The experiment's two parts are the guided plans.** *Part I* keeps the total mass at 200 g and
  moves 5 g from m₂ to m₁ each trial (100/100 → 120/80). *Part II* keeps the 10 g difference and adds
  10 g to both sides (50/60 → 90/100). Five trial slots per part, with the masses the procedure calls
  for shown greyed until you record them.
- **Both data tables are the experiment's** — trial, m₁, m₂, a, m_diff = m₁ − m₂ (kg), m_T (kg).
- **Analysis steps 1–5**, with both graphs: **a vs |Δm|** (Part I) is a straight line through the
  origin whose slope is compared against g/m_T, and **a vs m_T** (Part II) is plotted against the
  predicted curve while a·m_T is reported per trial. Step 5 writes out the combination,
  **a = |Δm|g / m_T**.
- **All five extensions are answered live:** free-body diagrams with both Newton's-second-law
  equations and the algebra that gives a = Δm g/m_T; expected versus measured trial by trial; an
  unknown mass on the left, solved from a = m₂(g − a)/(g + a) and then revealed; the tension on both
  sides; and the force the pulley feels, 2T against the total weight.
- **Ideal / realistic** toggle. Realistic adds the pulley's rotational inertia (as an equivalent
  mass) and its bearing friction, both adjustable, so the fitted acceleration comes out a few percent
  low — which is what the experiment's second extension question is about. A machine whose driving
  force is below the bearing friction correctly refuses to move.

## Notes

- Saved under the `atwood-lab-v1` localStorage key, with the theme at `atwood-lab-theme`.
- Models **PHY1510 Exp 07 – Atwood's Machine**. The pulley is drawn oversized so it reads on screen,

+# Atwood's Machine Lab · Photogate
+
+Two masses on either side of a pulley, connected by a light string, timed with a photogate. Fit
+velocity against time to get the acceleration, then relate that acceleration to the mass difference
+and to the total mass.
+
+**Run it:** open [index.html](index.html) in any browser. It is one self-contained file — no build
+step, no dependencies, works offline and on a phone. Dark/light is the button in the header and is
+remembered.
+
+## What it does
+
+- **The apparatus:** a ring stand and clamp holding a pulley with a photogate straddling its rim,
+  two masses hanging from the string and a cm ruler showing the descent. Release the masses and the
+  heavier side falls while the pulley spins and the gate pulses once per spoke.
+- **The photogate is the measurement.** Velocity is sampled once every tenth of a turn of the pulley
+  — one sample per 1.60 cm of string, what the Ultra Pulley's 10-spoke groove gives — and a
+  least-squares line is fitted to those points, as the *Curve Fit → Linear* step does. The slope is
+  the acceleration; the fit's intercept, r² and sample count (about 28 per run) are reported.
+- **The experiment's two parts are the guided plans.** *Part I* keeps the total mass at 200 g and
+  moves 5 g from m₂ to m₁ each trial (100/100 → 120/80). *Part II* keeps the 10 g difference and adds
+  10 g to both sides (50/60 → 90/100). Five trial slots per part, with the masses the procedure calls
+  for shown greyed until you record them.
+- **Both data tables are the experiment's** — trial, m₁, m₂, a, m_diff = m₁ − m₂ (kg), m_T (kg).
+- **Analysis steps 1–5**, with both graphs: **a vs |Δm|** (Part I) is a straight line through the
+  origin whose slope is compared against g/m_T, and **a vs m_T** (Part II) is plotted against the
+  predicted curve while a·m_T is reported per trial. Step 5 writes out the combination,
+  **a = |Δm|g / m_T**.
+- **All five extensions are answered live:** free-body diagrams with both Newton's-second-law
+  equations and the algebra that gives a = Δm g/m_T; expected versus measured trial by trial; an
+  unknown mass on the left, solved from a = m₂(g − a)/(g + a) and then revealed; the tension on both
+  sides; and the force the pulley feels, 2T against the total weight.
+- **Ideal / realistic** toggle. Realistic adds the pulley's rotational inertia (as an equivalent
+  mass) and its bearing friction, both adjustable, so the fitted acceleration comes out a few percent
+  low — which is what the experiment's second extension question is about. A machine whose driving
+  force is below the bearing friction correctly refuses to move.
+
+## Notes
+
+- Saved under the `atwood-lab-v1` localStorage key, with the theme at `atwood-lab-theme`.
+- Models **PHY1510 Exp 07 – Atwood's Machine**. The pulley is drawn oversized so it reads on screen,
+  but its rotation and spoke rate follow a real 1-inch radius, and travel is limited to 40–60 cm
+  because the masses must be able to move at least 40 cm before the falling one strikes the floor.
+- Listed in the site hub (`index.html` at the repository root) as **Atwood's Machine Lab**.
+- Previously served from `physics/atwood-machine.html`; that path now redirects here.

+# Circuit Lab · Draw & Measure
+
+A circuit board you draw on: place wire, resistors, batteries, capacitors, inductors, voltmeters,
+ammeters and switches on a grid, set their values, and read the meters live when the circuit is
+closed.
+
+**Run it:** open [index.html](index.html) in any browser. It is one self-contained file — no build
+step, no dependencies, no network access, works offline and on a phone. Dark/light is the button in
+the header and is remembered.
+
+## What it does
+
+- **Parts palette** — wire, resistor, battery, capacitor, inductor, voltmeter, ammeter and switch,
+  plus a current-direction arrow. Rotate, delete or undo a part, and click any part to edit it in
+  the inspector.
+- **Drawing mode** shows only the circuit elements: no meter readings and no current arrows, so you
+  can lay out and label a diagram.
+- **Simulation mode** closes the circuit: the voltmeter and ammeter show their readings and the
+  current arrows appear.
+- **Ideal / realistic** toggle for the simulation. Realistic gives each element 1–2 % of internal
+  resistance, so the meters no longer read the textbook values.
+- **Values you set:** a battery's voltage, a resistor's resistance and the current. Voltmeters read
+  the potential difference across the part they are placed over; ammeters read the current through
+  the branch they sit in.
+- **Board size** is adjustable — add or remove rows and columns, and the grid rescales.
+- **Export the drawing** as an image, and give any element a **custom label**.
+- Every change is kept in the browser, so a board survives a reload.
+
+## Notes
+
+- Saved under the `circuit-lab-board-v1` localStorage key, with the theme at `circuit-lab-theme`.
+- Listed in the site hub (`index.html` at the repository root) as **Circuit Diagram Builder**.

+# Torque Balance Lab · Meterstick Equilibrium
+
+A 100.0 cm meterstick on a knife-edge fulcrum with masses hanging from it. Move a hanger along the
+stick or move the fulcrum until the torques balance — τ = r·m·g taken about the pivot — with the
+stick's own weight acting at its center of gravity.
+
+**Run it:** open [index.html](index.html) in any browser. It is one self-contained file — no build
+step, no dependencies, works offline and on a phone. Dark/light is the button in the header and is
+remembered.
+
+## What it does
+
+- **Drag anything on the stick**, or tap it and fine-tune with a 0.1 cm slider and ±0.1 / ±1 nudges.
+  Move the fulcrum the same way.
+- **The cases from the experiment** are preloaded — Case 1, 2(a), 2(b), 3, 5 and 6(a)–(d) — each
+  with its procedure and its own apparatus setup, plus a free-explore mode.
+- **Torques about the fulcrum** are shown with the lever arms drawn on the stick and coloured by
+  side. The stick is a uniform ruler, so its weight acts at its centre of gravity whenever the
+  pivot is not there (Case 5).
+- **"Level it"** solves whichever element that case leaves free: the position of a hanger or the
+  fulcrum itself.
+- **Predictions** where the experiment asks for them (2b, 6d): type your answer and *Check* reports
+  how far off you are before nudging you back to the torque equation.
+- **Unknown mass (Case 3)** hides one mass completely: its row and torque read `?`, the unknown
+  side's total and the percent difference are withheld, and the method of moments appears once you
+  balance it. *Weigh it on the lab balance* then reveals the true value.
+- **Data & torques table** — every mass, position, lever arm, side and torque, both sums, the
+  percent difference, and a toggle between N·m and g·cm. An optional view splits the stick into two
+  segments (Case 5b) to show the same torque a second way.
+- The stick mass, stick centre of gravity, hanger clamp mass and g are all editable, and everything
+  is kept in the browser across reloads.
+
+## Notes
+
+- Saved under the `torque-lab-v1` localStorage key, with the theme at `torque-lab-theme`.
+- Models **PHY1510 Exp 08 – Torques, Equilibrium, and Center of Mass**.
+- Listed in the site hub (`index.html` at the repository root) as **Torque Balance Lab**.
+- Previously served from `physics/torque-balance.html`; that path now redirects here.

+# Work & Power Lab · Cart on an Incline
+
+A cart on an inclined board, pulled up the board by a weight hanging over a pulley. Release the
+cart, time the run, and then work out the force, work, power and the energy bookkeeping.
+
+**Run it:** open [index.html](index.html) in any browser. It is one self-contained file — no build
+step, no dependencies, works offline and on a phone. Dark/light is the button in the header and is
+remembered.
+
+## What it does
+
+- **The rig:** a board on a stand with a pulley at the raised end, a cart on the board and a string
+  over the pulley to a hanging weight. Its length and raised-end height fix sinθ = H/L, and the
+  distance the cart travels is set by a draggable stop mark.
+- **Nine trials** — three mass groups × three trials, exactly as the experiment asks, with the
+  trials auto-advancing once a mass group is full.
+- **Two ways to time it:** **photo-gate** (the exact crossing time) or **stopwatch**, where you tap
+  Stop and your reaction time becomes part of the reading. Letting the cart run off the end without
+  stopping it voids the trial.
+- **The forces on the cart are drawn** — the pull from the hanging weight, the cart's weight along
+  the slope and, in Realistic mode, rolling resistance — so it is visible why the cart only breaks
+  free once the hanging weight beats m·g·sinθ + f. The app names the threshold.
+- **Record sheet** reproducing the experiment's data table: mass added, total mass, three trial
+  times and their average, plus the hanger mass, distance travelled, rise and cart mass.
+- **Post-lab analysis** per mass with the arithmetic shown: v<sub>avg</sub> = d/t̄, a = 2d/t̄²,
+  v<sub>f</sub> = 2d/t̄, F = m g, W = F d, P = W/t, W<sub>cons</sub> = ΔPE = m<sub>cart</sub> g h,
+  ΔKE = ½m<sub>cart</sub>v<sub>f</sub>², and whether the system comes out conservative — including
+  splitting the leftover energy into friction and the stopwatch's timing error.
+- **Ideal / realistic** toggle with an adjustable rolling-resistance coefficient, and a g input.
+
+## Notes
+
+- Saved under the `workpower-lab-v1` localStorage key, with the theme at `workpower-lab-theme`.
+- Models **PHY1510 Exp 06a – Work and Power**.
+- Listed in the site hub (`index.html` at the repository root) as **Work & Power Lab (incline)**.
+- Previously served from `physics/work-power-lab.html`; that path now redirects here.

- **The apparatus:** a ring stand and clamp holding a Vernier Ultra Pulley with a photogate straddling its rim, two masses hanging from the string, and a cm ruler showing the descent. Release the masses and the heavier side falls, the pulley spins, and the gate flashes every time a spoke passes.
- **The photogate is the measurement.** Velocity is sampled every tenth of a turn of the pulley — one sample per 1.60 cm of string, which is what the Ultra Pulley's 10-spoke groove gives — and a least-squares line is fitted to those points, exactly as the LabQuest *Curve Fit → Linear* step asks. The slope is reported as the acceleration, with the intercept, r² and the sample count. About 28 points per run.
- **The file's two parts are the guided plans:** Part I keeps the total at 200 g and moves 5 g from m₂ to m₁ (100/100 → 120/80), Part II keeps the 10 g difference and adds 10 g to both sides (50/60 → 90/100). Progress note:
Done — both readings in the Work & Power Lab now carry ±0.5% scatter.

**The change** is in [work-power/index.html](work-power/index.html), applied at the single point where a reading is recorded, so it covers both modes:

```js
var JITTER = 0.005;
function reading(t) { return t * (1 + (Math.random() * 2 - 1) * JITTER); }
```

`finishRun()` now records `round3(reading(t))`. That one function is the recording path for both timers — the photo-gate calls it with the exact crossing time, and the stopwatch's Stop calls it with the real elapsed time — so the photo-gate reading gets ±0.5%, and the stopwatch gets your reaction time *plus* ±0.5% on top.

I also corrected the copy that claimed the photo-gate was exact, since it no longer is: the note under the record sheet, the "running" line for the photo-gate (now says it reads the crossing time to about ±0.5 %), the advice after a run off the end of the board, the energy-balance verdict (it now says the balance closes *to within the ±0.5 % scatter of the timing*), and the footer. [README.md](work-power/README.md) was updated to match.

**Verified in the browser**

- Photo-gate, nine real trials across the three masses: 0.782 / 0.780 / 0.782 (true crossing 0.782 s), 0.620 / 0.624 / 0.621 (0.621 s), 0.548 / 0.546 / 0.549 (0.546 s). Eight of the nine values are distinct — repeated trials of one mass now differ, where before all three came out identical.
- Stopwatch, three taps at the same point: recorded 0.618 / 0.627 / 0.632 s against the elapsed times I measured at 0.621 / 0.625 / 0.629 s — deviations of −0.48 %, +0.32 % and +0.48 %, the ±0.5 % band sitting on top of the reaction time.
- The analysis propagates it: for Mass 1 with t<sub>avg</sub> = 0.781 s it now reports a = 1.641 m/s² (the exact value is 1.633), v<sub>f</sub> = 1.281 m/s, P = 1.569 W and ΔKE = 0.410 J, and the verdict still reads "The energy balance closes… to within the ±0.5 % scatter of the timing". No console errors, and the scripts parse.

One detail worth knowing: a displayed deviation can look slightly over 0.5 % — for instance a reading of 0.549 s against a true 0.546 s reads as +0.549 %. That is rounding, not a wider band: the times are shown to the nearest millisecond, so both the reading and the true time are quantised before the comparison. The scatter itself is strictly within ±0.5 %.

Progress note:
Fixed — it was two bugs in the board drawing, and neither was in the physics.

**Bug 1: the displacement was 100× too small.** `tick()` computed the travel in metres (`0.5·a·t²`) but every consumer of that value treats it as centimetres: the drawing lifts the masses by `x · PPC` (PPC = 3.4 units per cm), the descent label appends "cm", and the pulley angle divides by 100 to get back to metres before dividing by the radius. So a 45 cm descent moved the masses **1.5 drawing units** instead of **150** — invisible — and the pulley turned 2.8° instead of 2.8 turns. The displacement is now in cm at the source, which is what the three places reading it already assumed.

**Bug 2: the falling mass never translated.** With `falls1` true, the code set `lowTop = BOT0 - g1.total` — the *start* level — while its bottom moved down to `lowY`. So the falling stack kept its top pinned and stretched downward instead of dropping: measured 94 → 231 px tall at a constant `y`. (The rising side happened to be right.) The top/bottom assignment is now per side — falling side bottom `lowY`, rising side `highBottom`, each top derived from its own bottom — and the equal-mass case still rests both stacks on the start line.

**Measured frame by frame, 120 g / 100 g, original layout scale** ([atwood-machine/index.html](atwood-machine/index.html))

| | before | after the run |
| --- | --- | --- |
| m₁ (falls) | bottom 556, height 94 | y 462 → 588, height **94 constant** |
| m₂ (rises) | bottom 556, height 82 | y 474 → 348, height **82 constant** |
| descent readout | 0.0 cm | 0.6 → 3.1 → 5.8 → 11.7 → 19.5 → 25.9 → 37.0 cm |
| pulley rotation | 0° | −13° → −836° (≈ 2.3 turns, 45 cm on a 1-inch groove) |

Their bottoms start level at 556 and the run ends at the catch line; the 45 cm travel is essentially all drawn (the final ~1 cm falls inside the last frame before the run ends). Reverse direction (100 g / 150 g) also translates cleanly now — m₂ falls 443 → 575, m₁ rises 474 → 342, both heights constant — and with equal masses both stacks stay put at the start line. Phone-width compact mode animates the same way, with no horizontal scroll.

**Physics and data are untouched:** 120/100 still fits a = 0.891 m/s² against its 0.891 prediction, 120/80 fits 1.960 against 1.960, **Record trial** still writes the trial into the table and storage, and there are no console errors. The desktop layout from the previous step is unchanged.

Two things worth knowing. The board returns to the start pose when the run ends (the app draws a "caught after 45 cm" line rather than leaving the masses where they stopped) — say the word if you'd rather they stay at the caught position. And my earlier check of this app was not good enough: the recorded data and the fit were correct, so a passing run looked like proof the animation worked, when the drawing path was broken. I also had to re-measure in a fresh browser tab, because the first tab stopped producing animation frames entirely.

I left the saved state at its defaults (100/100 g, no trials) and nothing is committed.

**The ±0.1 cm control**

The Controls card already had ±0.1 pills for the pivot and the selected hanger, but they sit several hundred pixels below the board — the button row measured at y ≈ 1137 on a 900 px-tall window — so they were easy to miss. Rather than duplicate them, I put a **fine-move bar under the stick** that appears whenever something is selected:

`[m1] 15.0 cm            −1  −0.1  +0.1  +1`

- It shows the selected element — the hanger's role or **Fulcrum** — with its live position, so you can see the effect without scrolling.
- **−0.1 / +0.1** step by exactly 0.1 cm; −1 / +1 are still there for coarse moves. Steps round to 0.1 cm and clamp to the 0–100 cm stick (`0.0` and `100.0` measured at the ends).
- Keyboard: **← / →** move the selection 0.1 cm, **Shift + ← / →** move 1 cm. Keys are ignored while you're typing in a number field, and with Ctrl/Cmd/Alt held. The keyboard hint hides below 560 px, since a phone has no arrow keys.
- It's in the sticky stage, so the bar stays on screen at 52 px tall on a phone (39 px tap targets) and 91 px on desktop including the hint.
- It shares one implementation with the card, so both stay in sync: nudging from either place updates the stick, the Controls slider, the chips, the table and the saved state (verified: 15.0 → 14.9 → 14.8 → 14.7 with −0.1 three times, then 15.7 with +1, and the stored item read `x: 15.7`).

**Mass labels outside the weight**

- The block is only 30–84 viewBox units wide — a 100 g block is 34 — while "100 g" at 19 px is 47 units, so the mass is now drawn **under the block** in the side's colour, with the `x = … cm` line beneath it. The role (m1, m2 …) stays on the block.
- Block minimum width raised from 30 to 46 units, because the role text itself was 42 units wide for a 34-unit block and was spilling out. Now it fits (30 ≤ 46).
- Spacing measured: block → mass 6.3 units, mass → x label 3.6, x label → selection ring 2.9, with no box overlap.
- Because the label hangs below the weight, a heavy mass near the end of the stick would have been cut off by the 500-unit viewBox (measured: ink to 567). The board now grows its viewBox to the deepest reach its hangers can have at full tilt — only when needed. **The ±0.1 cm control**

The Controls card already had ±0.1 pills for the pivot and the selected hanger, but they sit several hundred pixels below the board — the button row measured at y ≈ 1137 on a 900 px-tall window — so they were easy to miss. Rather than duplicate them, I put a **fine-move bar under the stick** that appears whenever something is selected:

`[m1] 15.0 cm            −1  −0.1  +0.1  +1`

- It shows the selected element — the hanger's role or **Fulcrum** — with its live position, so you can see the effect without scrolling.
- **−0.1 / +0.1** step by exactly 0.1 cm; −1 / +1 are still there for coarse moves. Steps round to 0.1 cm and clamp to the 0–100 cm stick (`0.0` and `100.0` measured at the ends).
- Keyboard: **← / →** move the selection 0.1 cm, **Shift + ← / →** move 1 cm. Keys are ignored while you're typing in a number field, and with Ctrl/Cmd/Alt held. The keyboard hint hides below 560 px, since a phone has no arrow keys.
- It's in the sticky stage, so the bar stays on screen at 52 px tall on a phone (39 px tap targets) and 91 px on desktop including the hint.
- It shares one implementation with the card, so both stay in sync: nudging from either place updates the stick, the Controls slider, the chips, the table and the saved state (verified: 15.0 → 14.9 → 14.8 → 14.7 with −0.1 three times, then 15.7 with +1, and the stored item read `x: 15.7`).

**Mass labels outside the weight**

- The block is only 30–84 viewBox units wide — a 100 g block is 34 — while "100 g" at 19 px is 47 units, so the mass is now drawn **under the block** in the side's colour, with the `x = … cm` line beneath it. The role (m1, m2 …) stays on the block.
- Block minimum width raised from 30 to 46 units, because the role text itself was 42 units wide for a 34-unit block and was spilling out. Now it fits (30 ≤ 46).
- Spacing measured: block → mass 6.3 units, mass → x label 3.6, x label → selection ring 2.9, with no box overlap.
- Because the label hangs below the weight, a heavy mass near the end of the stick would have been cut off by the 500-unit viewBox (measured: ink to 567). The board now grows its viewBox to the deepest reach its hangers can have at full tilt — only when needed. Done. The stick is now one fixed 89.5 g metre stick in every case, shown in **Apparatus** and printed on the board.

**What changed** ([torque-balance/index.html](torque-balance/index.html))

- **One mass for all cases.** The per-session random draw (88.5–90.5 g) is gone, replaced by a single `STICK_MASS = 89.5` used by the state, the case loader, Case 6(d)'s computed pivot and the fallback when the field is cleared. Loading any case leaves it untouched, so Cases 1 → 6(d) all hang the same stick.
- **Apparatus shows it correctly.** The *Stick mass (g)* field is refreshed from the live value on every render, formatted to one decimal (it was echoing whatever was in state; now it always matches what the physics uses — the data table's `meterstick at CG` row reads the same 89.5).
- **The board labels the stick.** A small `stick 89.5 g` caption sits at the top-left of the animation panel, above the stick's left end, and updates with the mass. It is deliberately outside the rotating beam group: the band between the beam and the lever-arm dimensions is only ~22 units tall on desktop and the dimension rows swing up into it at full tilt, so a label on the stick would have collided. Placed at the top-left it clears everything at any pose.
- **Old saves migrate once.** The saved-state version went 4 → 5. A setup stored by the previous build adopts 89.5 on its next load; from then on a value you type is saved and kept. Without this, an existing browser would have kept showing its old random 90.2 g forever.
- Editing the field still applies everywhere: typing **150** gave `stick 150 g` on the board, `150` in the table, and Case 6(d) opened at **44.3 cm** — the 150 g answer — instead of 43.1 cm.

| Overlap with CG text, ruler numbers, dimension labels, pivot label | none, in every case |
| Max tilt (2000 g hanger, 11°) | label top 174 px vs nearest dimension label 210 px — no overlap |
| Phone (390, compact) | label 28 px class, inside the board, no horizontal scroll |
| Old v4 save with 90.2 g → reload | becomes 89.5, saved as v5 |
| Typed 150 g → reload | still 150 (v5 saves edits) |
| Console | no errors; main script parses |

Case 6(d) now opens at **43.1 cm**, which is 6(c)'s balance for an 89.5 g stick. [README.md](torque-balance/README.md) documents the single-mass rule and the board label. I cleared the saved state at the end, so the app opens fresh in Case 1, and nothing is committed.
